claim: Zhao et al. claimed that sexual selection produces the multimodal displays seen in little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis) by co-opting limb movements that originally evolved to support parasite defense.
source: Zhao et al. recently reported results which, they claim, suggest that sexual selection produces the multimodal displays seen in little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis) by co-opting limb movements that originally evolved to support parasite defense (Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is attributed to Zhao et al., 2022 through citation.

claim: Many animals communicate by performing multimodal displays that showcase vocal and gestural signals.
source: Many animals communicate by performing multimodal displays that showcase vocal and gestural signals (Partan and Marler, 1999; Bro-Jørgensen, 2010; Higham and Hebets, 2013; Starnberger et al., 2014b; Mitoyen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis) inhabit noisy streams throughout Hainan Island in Southern China.
source: They did this by studying little torrent frogs (Amolops torrentis), which inhabit noisy streams throughout Hainan Island in Southern China (Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2022.

claim: Zhao et al. concluded that male frogs produce a set of discrete arm and leg maneuvers to help swat away blood-sucking parasites.
source: They concluded that: (i) male frogs produce a set of discrete arm and leg maneuvers to help swat away blood-sucking parasites
evidence: This is a summary of conclusions from Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: Zhao et al. concluded that limb movements enhance the attractiveness of male calls to females.
source: (ii) these same limb movements enhance the attractiveness of male calls to females.
evidence: This is a summary of conclusions from Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: Only limb shaking (LSA) and wiping (W) were more likely to occur in the presence of parasites than expected by chance.
source: We therefore ran such an analysis, and we found that only two movements —limb shaking (LSA) and wiping (W)—were more likely to occur in the presence of parasites than one might expect by chance (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' reanalysis of data from Zhao et al., with results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Limb shaking (LSA) and wiping (W) were not the movements that females preferred in choice tests.
source: Importantly, these specific movements were not the ones that females preferred in choice tests (Figure 5C and 5D in Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim references data from Zhao et al., 2022, specifically Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Hind foot lifting (HFL) and arm wiping (AW) were not more likely to occur in the presence of parasites.
source: At the same time, we found that both hind foot lifting (HFL) and arm wiping (AW) were not more likely to occur in the presences of parasites (Figure 1)
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' reanalysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Hind foot lifting (HFL) and arm wiping (AW) were the two limb movements that females seemed to prefer in choice tests.
source: even though these were the two limb movements that females seemed to prefer in choice tests (Figure 5A and 5B in Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim references data from Zhao et al., 2022, specifically Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Parasite presence is associated with only certain limb movements that are not positively linked to female preference.
source: Our results therefore suggest that parasite presence is associated with only certain limb movements that Zhao et al. studied, but none that are positively linked to female preference
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the authors' reanalysis of the data.

claim: Correlation does not equal causation.
source: However, correlation does not equal causation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific principle.

claim: Higher quality males who display more vigorously may occupy spots along the breeding stream that contain more parasites.
source: Other explanations for the association include the possibility that higher quality males who display more vigorously also occupy spots along the breeding stream that contain more parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Micro- and macro-ecological factors that determine the abundance and distribution of blood-sucking parasites that target frogs are poorly understood.
source: Micro- and macro-ecological factors that determine the abundance and distribution of blood-sucking parasites that target frogs are poorly understood (outlined recently by Virgo et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Virgo et al., 2022.

claim: A wide range of factors associated with the local landscape and ecology can influence the distribution and abundance of midges.
source: but other work in midges implies a wide range of factors associated with the local landscape and ecology can influence their distribution and abundance (Kluiters et al., 2013; Rigot et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on midges.

claim: Parasites might be attracted to male calls.
source: Alternatively, parasites might be attracted to male calls (Bernal et al., 2006; Aihara et al., 2016; Toma et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Males might produce calls more often when they are using their limbs to display during bouts of male-male competition.
source: which males might produce more often when they are using their limbs to display during bouts of male-male competition (Grafe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grafe et al., 2012.

claim: Most frogs that use gestural signals do so for male-male competition purposes.
source: Most frogs that use gestural signals do so for this purpose (see Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Table 1 which lists anuran species and their limb display behaviors.

claim: Gestural signals in frogs are assumed to evolve through intrasexual selection.
source: and thus the behavior is assumed to evolve through intrasexual selection (Preininger et al., 2013b; Preininger et al., 2013c; Mangiamele and Fuxjager, 2018; Anderson et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Little torrent frogs use limb movements in male-male interaction contexts.
source: but they do indicate that little torrent frogs use these movements in such contexts.
evidence: This is an inference from Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: There are currently no studies that clearly and definitively show that male frogs use the same limb movements described by Zhao et al. to attract female mates.
source: To our knowledge, there are currently no studies that clearly and definitively show that male frogs use the same limb movements described by Zhao et al. to attract female mates.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Observational evidence for visual displays employed during courtship in frogs is relatively rare and functionally ambiguous.
source: There is certainly some observational evidence for visual displays employed during courtship, but such data are relatively rare and functionally ambiguous (examples: de Sá et al., 2018 has n=3 courtship interactions; Furtado et al., 2019 has n=1 courtship interaction).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies with limited sample sizes.

claim: Zhao et al. only reported four male-female interactions across two breeding seasons.
source: To this end, Zhao et al. only report four male-female interactions across two breeding seasons
evidence: This is a statement about data from Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: During male-female interactions in Zhao et al.'s study, males did not produce any of the limb displays purported to be linked with parasite defense.
source: and during these interactions males don't produce any of the limb displays that are purported to be linked with parasite defense.
evidence: This is a statement about data from Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: It is nearly impossible to distinguish male gestural displays directed to other males from those directed at females when working in the field with torrent frogs.
source: Furthermore, when working in the field with torrent frogs, one must recognize that it is nearly impossible to distinguish male gestural displays directed to other males from those directed at females (see Table 1 and most "courtship" interactions listed therein).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge and reference to Table 1.

claim: Males in the area will trigger gestural behaviors from each other, even as females approach.
source: This is because males in the area will trigger these behaviors from each other, even as females approach (Preininger and Fuxjager, personal observations; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on personal observations and citation to Zhao et al., 2022.

claim: The video stimuli used by Zhao et al. are not ecologically relevant to female frogs.
source: However, these video stimuli are not ecologically relevant to female frogs.
evidence: This is a critical assessment by the authors of Zhao et al.'s experimental design.

claim: Each stimulus in Zhao et al.'s experiment was manually altered to include a standardized audio channel, such that the male in the video would be perceived to have called without inflating its vocal sac.
source: This is because each stimulus was manually altered to include a standardized audio channel, such that the male in the video would be perceived to have called without inflating its vocal sac.
evidence: This is a description of Zhao et al.'s experimental methods.

claim: Free-living females do not naturally encounter stimuli where males call without inflating their vocal sac, particularly when females assess males by looking at them head-on.
source: Free-living females do not naturally encounter such stimuli, particularly when they assess males by looking at them head-on (as females do in this experiment).
evidence: This is an inference about natural behavior based on the experimental setup.

claim: Vocal sac inflation has a powerful effect on sexual attractiveness and mate choice in frogs.
source: Vocal sac inflation has a powerful effect on sexual attractiveness and mate choice in frogs (reviewed by Starnberger et al., 2014a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Vocal sac inflation has a powerful effect on sexual attractiveness and mate choice in little torrent frogs.
source: including in little torrent frogs (Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2021.

claim: If vocal sac inflation masks effects of limb movements on female preference, then selection should not strongly favor the co-option of these movements into the display.
source: Importantly, if vocal sac inflation does mask effects of limb movements on female preference, then selection should not strongly favor the co-option of these movements into the display.
evidence: This is a logical inference about evolutionary selection.

claim: Females showed a preference for males that produced HFL and AW movements because they were the closest resemblance of "fixed" vocal sac inflations.
source: We suspect that females showed a preference for males that produced HFL and AW movements because they were the closest resemblance of "fixed" vocal sac inflations, particularly when the alternative stimulus included calls without vocal sac inflations (Rosenthal et al., 2004; Narins et al., 2005; Taylor et al., 2008; Gomez et al., 2011; Preininger et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Visual and acoustic components might differ in context and dominance, but nevertheless strongly modulate mate choice.
source: Visual and acoustic components might differ in context and dominance, but nevertheless strongly modulate mate choice (Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2011.

claim: Females can observe males producing limb movements and calls without seeing vocal sac inflation when females see males from behind.
source: One might argue against our point by saying that females can in fact observe males producing limb movements and calls without seeing vocal sac inflation, such as when females see males from behind.
evidence: This is a hypothetical counterargument presented by the authors.

claim: Visual perspectives of the male from behind were not incorporated into Zhao et al.'s experimental design.
source: However, such visual perspectives of the male were not incorporated into the experimental design, and thus the current study cannot reveal how females would respond to seeing males perform limb movements from such alternate angles.
evidence: This is a critique of Zhao et al.'s experimental design.

claim: Only certain limb movements are potentially performed more in the presence of parasites, and these are not the movements that females seem to prefer.
source: By reanalyzing data from this study, we show that only certain limb movements are potentially performed more in the presence of parasites, and these are not the movements that females seem to prefer.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' reanalysis results.

claim: Zhao et al. over-interprets correlational evidence to propose that limb movements evolved to avoid parasite attacks.
source: The study by Zhao et al. also over-interprets correlational evidence to propose that limb movements evolved to avoid parasite attacks.
evidence: This is a critical assessment by the authors.

claim: Zhao et al. cannot determine whether limb movements are functionally significant during male-female interactions because female preference experiments were limited with respect to their ethological relevance.
source: Finally, Zhao et al. cannot determine whether limb movements are functionally significant during male-female interactions because female preference experiments were limited with respect to their ethological relevance.
evidence: This is a critical assessment by the authors.

claim: Data videos and drawings of limb movements in Zhao et al.'s study are ambiguous and unclear.
source: For example, data videos and drawings of limb movements are ambiguous and unclear (e.g., parasites are unclear in Video 1; gesture illustrations in Figure 1E and C show mirror images of the same movements)
evidence: This is a critique of the quality of data presentation in Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: There are no data in Zhao et al.'s study showing how frequently frogs use limb movements to physically wipe away parasites.
source: and there are no data showing how frequently frogs use limb movements to physically wipe away parasites
evidence: This is a critique of missing data in Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: There are no data in Zhao et al.'s study showing whether frogs ever experience parasites in their "vicinity" without producing limb movements.
source: or whether frogs ever experience parasites in their "vicinity" without producing limb movements.
evidence: This is a critique of missing data in Zhao et al.'s study.

claim: It is unclear why preference tests in Zhao et al.'s study were carried out at night, which creates a temporal mismatch with day-recorded video stimuli.
source: It is also unclear why preference tests were carried out at night, which creates a temporal mismatch with day-recorded video stimuli.
evidence: This is a critique of Zhao et al.'s experimental design.

claim: Visual displays in frogs might arise through the co-option of adaptive movements that are unrelated to communication.
source: Nonetheless, as biologists who study gestural signals in frogs, we remain open to the possibility that visual displays might arise through the co-option of adaptive movements that are unrelated to communication.
evidence: This is a statement of openness to a hypothesis.

claim: The role of female choice in the evolution of frog limb displays is poorly understood and merits further investigation.
source: Similarly, we recognize that the role of female choice in the evolution of frog limb displays is poorly understood and merits further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Zhao et al. did not account for the drastic differences in number of behaviors produced by each frog.
source: For data preprocessing, we noted that Zhao et al. did not account for the drastic differences in number of behaviors produced by each frog.
evidence: This is a critique of Zhao et al.'s data analysis methods.

claim: Weighting values can be an important way to avoid certain individuals having an outsized effect on statistical outcomes.
source: Weighting values can be an important way to avoid such effects, and so we adopted this approach.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical methodology.

claim: Toe trembling is not a parasite defense behavior.
source: Past studies, including some that Zhao et al. cite (such as Hödl and Amézquita, 2001), show that toe trembling is not a parasite defense behavior
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Toe trembling is commonly used either as a social signal or as a feeding/hunger signal.
source: rather, it is commonly used either as a social signal (Lindquist and Hetherington, 1996; Rojas and Pašukonis, 2019) or as a feeding/hunger signal (Grafe, 2008; Hagman and Shine, 2008; Sloggett and Zeilstra, 2008; McFadden et al., 2010; Claessens et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Limb shaking behavior (LSA) was statistically significantly more likely to occur in the presence of parasites (χ2=5.0314, P=0.025).
source: We found that (E) limb shaking behavior (LSA) was statistically significant (χ2=5.0314, P=0.025, denoted with asterisk)
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' statistical analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Wiping (W) was statistically significantly more likely to occur in the presence of parasites (χ2=4.212, P=0.040).
source: as was (F) wiping (W) (χ2=4.212, P=0.040, denoted with asterisk).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' statistical analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Toe trembling (TT) was not statistically significantly more likely to occur in the presence of parasites (χ2=0.084, P=0.772).
source: We found that (B) toe trembling (TT) was (as expected) not statistically significant (χ2=0.084, P=0.772)
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' statistical analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Hind foot lifting (HFL) was not statistically significantly more likely to occur in the presence of parasites (χ2=0.487, P=0.485).
source: nor was (C) hind foot lifting (HFL; χ2=0.487, P=0.485)
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' statistical analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Arm wiping (AW) was not statistically significantly more likely to occur in the presence of parasites (χ2=2.772, P=0.096).
source: or (D) arm wiping (AW; χ2=2.772, P=0.096).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' statistical analysis shown in Figure 1.
